subject: literature
passage: "I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud," a poem by William Wordsworth first published in 1807 and revised for an 1815 edition, recalls a walk on which the speaker came upon a great crowd of daffodils beside a lake. Much of the poem lingers on the scene itself: the flowers' numbers, their motion in the breeze, and the sparkling water beside them. Yet the speaker also suggests that the encounter did not end on the day of the walk, since the daffodils return to him afterward, when he is by himself, and continue to affect him.
stem: Which quotation from "I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud" most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.A: "I gazed—and gazed—but little thought / What wealth the show to me had brought:"
choices.B: "They flash upon that inward eye / Which is the bliss of solitude;"
choices.C: "Continuous as the stars that shine / And twinkle on the milky way,"
choices.D: "The waves beside them danced; but they / Out-did the sparkling waves in glee:"

explanation.why: The claim has two parts: the daffodils come back to the speaker later, and they do so when he is alone. The quotation must show both. In "They flash upon that inward eye / Which is the bliss of solitude," the flowers reappear in his memory (his "inward eye") during "solitude."
explanation.A: Incorrect. This hints that the scene was worth more than the speaker realized at the time, but it does not show the flowers returning to him when he is alone.
explanation.B: Correct. The daffodils reappear in the speaker's memory, his "inward eye," and the lines place that moment in "solitude," so both parts of the claim are shown.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This line describes the daffodils as they looked during the walk, comparing them to stars; it says nothing about their returning to him later.
explanation.D: Incorrect. These lines describe the scene during the walk, comparing the flowers with the waves; they do not show the encounter continuing afterward.

source.author: William Wordsworth
source.work: I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud
